title: ORION: Decoupling and Alignment for Unified Autoregressive Understanding and Generation
one_liner: ORION keeps one autoregressive model for both image understanding and image generation, but separates low-level image reconstruction pressure from the shared semantic representation and then explicitly aligns them during generation.
lead: A unified multimodal model should answer questions about an image and also generate images or image tokens from text. In a monolithic autoregressive model, meaning one model that predicts the next item in a sequence for every task, those goals fight each other. Image generation pushes the shared representation toward local pixel reconstruction details, while understanding needs abstract meaning that stays stable across wording, layout, and visual surface changes. ORION keeps the simple one-model design but adds two controls: a dedicated non-linear vision head to carry the structural burden of generation, and a representation consistency loss that preserves the semantic representation while generation is trained.

problem.h2: Why one model forgets understanding when it learns generation
paras: Understanding and generation use the same input stream but demand different internal features. For visual question answering, the model needs a semantic representation, meaning a list of numbers that preserves category, relation, and intent. For autoregressive image generation, the model must also preserve local structure needed to predict the next visual token, meaning the next discrete code in an image sequence.

If the same hidden states carry both jobs with no separation, generation training can dominate because predicting the next visual token rewards short-range reconstruction detail. The model then spends capacity on surface regularities and its understanding features drift. That is the semantic-structural conflict described by the paper.

callout.html: ORION routes generation-specific structural pressure through a separate vision head and adds an alignment loss on the shared hidden states, because that extra head absorbs reconstruction detail while the alignment term resists semantic drift in the shared representation.

panels.title: 1. One backbone serves two jobs
panels.caption: A single autoregressive backbone feeds both question answering and image generation.

panels.title: 2. Generation pushes on local structure
panels.caption: Predicting the next visual code rewards local reconstruction detail more directly than high-level meaning.

panels.title: 3. Decouple with a vision head
panels.viz_args: shared hidden state -> non-linear vision head -> visual prediction
panels.caption: The extra head carries the structural conversion needed for generation, so the shared hidden state does not have to store all of it directly.

panels.title: 4. Align semantics during generation
panels.caption: A consistency loss keeps the shared representation close to the one that supports understanding.

panels.title: 5. One model keeps both skills
panels.caption: The model can answer and generate because the two pressures are organized instead of mixed blindly.

steps.text: Use one sequence model for multimodal inputs and outputs so both understanding and generation live in a common training pipeline.
Before predicting visual tokens, pass the shared hidden state through a dedicated mapping that can absorb low-level visual reconstruction demands.

steps.b: Run understanding tasks on the shared state
steps.text: Question answering, caption interpretation, and related tasks read from the shared hidden representation rather than from the generation head.
During generation training, penalize drift between the shared semantic representation and its intended understanding-oriented form so generation updates do not erase meaning.

steps.b: Train progressively on curated multimodal data
steps.text: Stage the data and task mix because early understanding-heavy training builds a stable semantic base, and later generation-heavy training can then add visual output skill with less drift in the shared state.

paras: The paper changes where structural image detail is represented. Instead of forcing the shared backbone state to simultaneously store semantic meaning and next-token reconstruction detail, ORION offloads much of that structural burden into a separate vision head and explicitly adds a penalty term that keeps the backbone state semantically stable.

hidden.name: semantic stability (how much the shared hidden state keeps the same meaning after generation loss updates it)
paras: The hidden quantity is not the image itself. It is the content of the shared hidden representation after the model has been trained to generate visual tokens. If that representation changes its meaning each time generation training raises local reconstruction quality, understanding performance drops because the answer path reads from the altered shared state.

ORION measures and controls this with representation consistency. The idea is direct: if two training views correspond to the same semantic content, then the shared hidden states should stay close even when one path is optimized for generation. Keeping that closeness matters because the answer head depends on stable meaning features, not on patch-level reconstruction detail.

heat.caption: The darker cells are the parts of the shared state that understanding needs to stay stable while generation training adds structural image detail elsewhere.

reads.html: The backbone should keep representing what is in the scene and what the instruction asks for, even while another part of the model learns how to write the visual output codes.

Representation consistency aligns the shared hidden states during generation, so semantic information remains usable for understanding instead of being overwritten by structural reconstruction pressure.

mechanism.h2: Why decoupling and alignment solve the conflict
paras: Generation and understanding disagree mainly about where to spend representational capacity. Visual generation needs details that are predictive for the next code in the image stream. Understanding needs abstractions that survive across many possible renderings. ORION resolves that conflict by placing a non-linear conversion layer between the backbone and visual token prediction. That layer can learn the mapping from semantic state to generation-ready structure, so the backbone does not need to carry every reconstruction cue directly.

The consistency loss is the second half of the solution. Decoupling alone would still allow generation update signals to drift the backbone in ways that hurt understanding. The alignment penalty counters that drift because it punishes changes to the shared hidden state that are not needed for preserving semantic content. With both pieces present, the backbone stores meaning, the vision head expands meaning into generation structure, and the monolithic autoregressive design remains intact.

stages.s: mixed multimodal sequence for question answering or generation
shared autoregressive backbone builds a semantic hidden representation
understanding tasks read the shared state directly
generation path passes through a non-linear vision head
representation consistency penalizes semantic drift during generation updates
one model that answers and generates without separate task-specific trainable numbers

math.words: Training combines the standard autoregressive generation loss with a consistency term that keeps the shared hidden representation close to a semantic target representation during generation updates.
symbols: autoregressive next-token prediction loss for multimodal outputs
representation consistency loss on the shared hidden states
weight that sets how strongly semantic stability is enforced during training

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose one batch gives L_AR = 0.90 and L_cons = 0.10.
If lambda_cons = 3, then the total is 0.90 + 3 * 0.10 = 1.20.
A batch with the same generation quality but L_cons = 0.30 would score 1.80, so training prefers updates that preserve the hidden semantic state.
That preference matters because the model is not rewarded only for predicting the next visual code correctly. It is also rewarded for keeping the shared representation usable for understanding.

math.note: The added term does not replace generation learning. It restricts how generation is allowed to alter the shared backbone state.

charts.title: Monolithic backbone without decoupling or alignment
charts.note: The plain design can learn generation detail, but understanding erodes because the shared hidden state absorbs conflicting pressure.

charts.title: ORION with vision head and consistency loss
charts.note: The extra head and alignment term keep one shared model while reducing the semantic damage caused by generation training.

items.b: The consistency term is too weak.
items.html: If the semantic penalty is underweighted, generation update signals still reshape the shared hidden state toward local visual prediction detail, and understanding quality drops for the same reason as in the plain monolithic design.

items.b: The vision head is too limited.
items.html: If the non-linear head cannot express the conversion from semantic state to generation-ready structure, the backbone must absorb that burden again and the conflict returns.

items.b: The training curriculum is poorly staged.
items.html: If generation-heavy data dominates before the shared semantic representation is stable, the model can lock into reconstruction shortcuts early and the later alignment term has less corrective influence.

The method works best when the backbone learns stable multimodal meaning first, the vision head has enough capacity to model generation structure, and the consistency weight is strong enough to resist semantic drift.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a compact multimodal autoregressive model that does two tasks on the same image-text data: answer a question about an image and generate image tokens from text. Train three versions: plain monolithic, monolithic plus vision head, and ORION with both the vision head and the consistency loss. After each generation-training phase, reevaluate image understanding on a held-out question-answer set.

The demo should show the paper's central claim directly: generation quality can rise without a matching collapse in understanding if structural reconstruction pressure is routed through a separate head and the shared semantic representation is held in place.
demo.closing: The key plot is retention gap versus generation score. ORION should keep a smaller retention gap because it constrains where generation-specific information is stored.
